TRACK_34_RESULT — Enterprise-Scale Performance Profiling (Executor user14)

# Track 34 — Enterprise-Scale Performance Profiling

**Executor:** user14 · **Task:** task_2026-09-02_016 · **Parent epic:** task_2026-09-02_002 (BiasAperture Phase 2)
**Repo state audited:** github.com/Aaradhya-Dev-Tamrakar/BiasAperture, main (WP1–4 complete, WP5 ~90%, verified 10,954-image FairFace-val run)

## 0. Method note

All findings below are grounded in the actual committed code (file:line references throughout), not assumed architecture — per the epic's research standard. Runtime figures are order-of-magnitude extrapolations from the current verified 10,954-row run, not benchmarked at 10⁶–10⁷ scale (no such dataset or hardware was available for this research pass); they should be validated with a real profiling run before being treated as a committed spec number.

## 1. Where the pipeline bottlenecks first

Three candidate bottlenecks were named in the task: inference, dual-backend fairness computation, and the bootstrap CI step. Reading the actual implementation resolves this cleanly — it is not an even three-way split.

### 1a. Bootstrap CI is the dominant cost, and it scales worse than it needs to

`fairness/statistics.py::compute_stratified_bootstrap_ci` (lines 131–283) is called exactly 4 times per backend — once per Core-Four metric at the whole-dataset ("ALL") row (backends.py:138,181,232,278 for Fairlearn; mirrored AIF360 sites at backends.py:635,678,729,775). That's 8 bootstrap calls per audit run total, not one per subgroup — the per-subgroup rows (backends.py:307–443) use a cheap ±0.05 heuristic band instead of a real bootstrap, so subgroup count (126 intersectional bins today) does not multiply bootstrap cost. This is a materially different scaling story than the task's framing implied, worth stating precisely so Phase-2 planning doesn't over-index on subgroup cardinality as the risk factor.

What does scale badly is n (row count) inside each of those 8 calls:

- The docstring calls this "Vectorized Stratified BCa Bootstrap," but the implementation (statistics.py:191–207) is a serial Python `for _b in range(n_resamples)` loop — 1,000+ iterations, each doing a per-stratum rng.choice + np.concatenate + a full call into metric_fn, which itself re-derives group rates from scratch every replicate (compute_group_rates inside dpd_fn/eod_fn/eop_fn/dir_fn, backends.py:87–130). Cost per bootstrap call is ~O(n_resamples × n) in pure Python/NumPy-per-call overhead, not a single vectorized NumPy pass. At n=10,954 this is already measurable; at n=1–10M (the task's 10×–100× framing) this is the term that will dominate wall-clock, because it's the only step whose cost is O(resamples × n) with Python-loop constant factors rather than O(n) vectorized.
- The jackknife acceleration step (statistics.py:228–259) is already well-designed for scale: it correctly switches from O(n) leave-one-out (n ≤ 300) to a subsampled delete-d jackknife (d = n // 100, ~100 replicates regardless of n) above that threshold. No action needed — flagging as a design strength, not a gap, so it isn't accidentally "fixed" into something worse.

Fix path — the one concrete, no-tradeoff recommendation of this track: replace the hand-rolled loop with `scipy.stats.bootstrap(..., method='BCa', vectorized=True, batch=...)`. SciPy's own bootstrap implements the identical BCa method BiasAperture already uses, natively supports batched vectorized resample evaluation (docs.scipy.org/scipy.stats.bootstrap: "batch: number of resamples to process in each vectorized call to statistic... batch sizes >>1 tend to be faster when statistic is vectorized"), and accepts an rng for the same reproducibility guarantee seed=42 already gives. Requires making dpd_fn/eod_fn/eop_fn/dir_fn accept an axis argument (vectorize compute_group_rates over a batch of resample index arrays instead of one at a time) — a real but bounded refactor of 4 functions, not a redesign. This changes zero statistical guarantees — same BCa method, same n_resamples ≥ 1000 (NFR-002), same alpha=0.05 (NFR-001) — it only removes the Python-loop tax.

### 1b. Dual-backend computation: not actually a compute bottleneck, but a trivially fixable wall-clock one

cli.py:126 runs "[*] Running dual-backend fairness estimation (Fairlearn + AIF360)..." as a single sequential step — grep across cli.py and backends.py finds no ThreadPool, multiprocessing, or joblib.Parallel anywhere in the codebase. FairlearnBackend and AIF360Backend are independent, side-effect-free, stateless computations over the same (y_true, y_pred, sensitive) arrays (per the project's own "Strategy pattern" framing in fairness/base.py) — an embarrassingly parallel pair with zero shared state. Running them sequentially in one process doubles wall-clock for no statistical reason. Easiest scale win available: wrap the two backend calls in concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor (2 workers) or joblib.Parallel(n_jobs=2) — no algorithmic change, no NFR impact, roughly halves total audit-run time regardless of dataset size.

### 1c. Inference (InProcessInterface) is out of current scope, but sets a precedent

InProcessInterface.get_predictions() is still NotImplementedError (model_interface.py:75–86) — inference-time cost only becomes relevant once Track 30 (Model-Agnostic Classifier Adapter Layer) lands. Flagging the dependency rather than speculating: at 10⁶–10⁷ scale, batched-GPU inference throughput will dominate total pipeline time if in-process inference is ever used, but that is Track 30's design surface, not this track's.

### Ranked bottleneck order at 10×–100× scale (predictions-file path, current architecture)

1. Bootstrap CI Python-loop overhead (§1a) — grows with n, currently masked because n=10,954 is small enough that 1,000 serial-Python resamples is sub-minute; will not stay masked at 10⁶+.
2. Dual-backend sequential execution (§1b) — constant 2× wall-clock penalty at every scale, cheap to remove, currently unaddressed.
3. CSV/JSON full-materialization ingestion (§2) — becomes a memory bottleneck (can OOM) before it's a compute bottleneck.
4. Per-subgroup chi-squared calls (backends.py:337–339, 126 bins × 2 backends = 252 calls) — each an O(n) contingency-table build; linear in n, not a structural risk, no action needed.

## 2. Batching / streaming ingestion strategies

model_interface.py::PredictionsFileInterface._load_rows (lines ~90–100) calls pd.read_csv(self.path) with no chunksize, then df.to_dict(orient="records") — this fully materializes the file twice: once as a pandas DataFrame, once as a Python list-of-dicts (to_dict is itself an O(n) allocation pass that roughly doubles peak memory versus reading the DataFrame alone). data_ingestion.py:183/204 does the identical pattern. At FairFace-val scale (10,954 rows) this is invisible; at millions of rows it is the first thing to OOM, well before bootstrap cost becomes painful.

Recommended fix, in order of effort vs. payoff (each fixes the ingestion memory problem without touching the schema or SubjectRecord/MetricResult contracts):

1. pd.read_csv(..., chunksize=N) + yield-per-chunk — smallest change (PredictionsFileInterface already yields SubjectRecord one at a time from get_predictions(), so the generator contract is already correct; only _load_rows needs to become a chunked generator instead of one to_dict call). Zero new dependencies.
2. Polars scan_csv (lazy) → .collect(streaming=True) or batched .iter_slices() — better memory/CPU profile than pandas chunking (independent 2025–2026 benchmarks report Polars using "30–60% less memory on large CSV workloads due to column pruning and streaming" and automatic multi-core parallelism vs. pandas' single-threaded, GIL-bound execution — Shuttle.dev benchmark, Sept 2025). Worth adopting as a new optional ingestion path (additive, doesn't replace the pandas path) if target client datasets are routinely in the 10⁶+ row range.
3. JSON path is the harder case — model_interface.py's JSON branch calls json.load(f) (whole file into memory as a Python object tree) with no streaming equivalent as clean as read_csv's chunksize. For very large JSON predictions files, line-delimited JSON (JSONL) + a line-by-line generator, or requiring CSV above a size threshold, is the pragmatic fix — don't over-invest in streaming-JSON tooling (ijson etc.) unless a real client need for huge JSON predictions files materializes.
4. Out of scope for this track but worth flagging for Track 32 (API-First Service Layer): a service-layer job model would want chunked ingestion paired with incremental progress reporting, not just a memory fix — a coordination point, not a duplication of Track 32's work.

## 3. Should bootstrap resample count or subgroup granularity ever be reduced for speed?

No, not as a default, and any reduction path must be explicit, logged, and opt-in — never silent.

- MIN_BOOTSTRAP_RESAMPLES = 1000 (NFR-002) and ALPHA = 0.05 (NFR-001) are constructor-level constants in schema.py, and compute_stratified_bootstrap_ci already hard-floors any caller-supplied n_resamples via max(n_resamples, MIN_BOOTSTRAP_RESAMPLES) (statistics.py:169). That floor is a real, already-enforced guarantee — Phase-2 work should preserve it verbatim, not relax it for a performance win. Similarly MIN_SUBGROUP_SAMPLE_SIZE = 30 (NFR-003) is enforced at MetricResult.__post_init__ construction time, not at report-render time — a subgroup-granularity "reduction for speed" would mean pre-aggregating bins before they reach MetricResult, which would just be a silent NFR-003 violation wearing a performance justification. This track finds no legitimate mechanism to reduce either without breaking a locked NFR, and recommends none.
- The correct axis for speed is parallelization of independent work, which this repo currently does zero of: §1a vectorize/batch the bootstrap resamples themselves (SciPy's own batch parameter) — same 1,000+ resamples computed, just not one Python object at a time; §1b run the two backends concurrently — same two full computations, just not sequentially in one process. Both are "resamples/backends computed in parallel," never "fewer resamples/backends computed."
- One nuance worth surfacing rather than resolving unilaterally: at genuinely enterprise scale, the jackknife acceleration step's delete-d subsampling (d = n // 100) means d itself grows with n (e.g., d ≈ 10,000 at n=1M) — each jackknife replicate then drops a much larger absolute slice per iteration. Mathematically consistent with the existing subsampled-jackknife literature the code already implements, but nobody has validated that the acceleration-parameter estimate stays well-behaved at that d. Flagging as an open validation question, not asserting it's a bug.

## 4. Cross-track synthesis

Strongest contribution: corrected bottleneck ranking (bootstrap Python-loop overhead > sequential dual-backend execution > ingestion memory, not an even three-way split) and a concrete, NFR-preserving fix for each of the first two.

Potential overlap: Track 32 (API-First Service Layer) will need the same ingestion-chunking work for its async job model — this track's §2 findings should feed it directly. Track 33 (Containerized Deployment) should size container memory limits assuming the current double-materializing ingestion pattern unless §2's fix lands first.

Potential conflict: none identified against Track 21 (Streaming Audit Mode) — compatible with, and arguably needs, the same chunked-ingestion and parallel-backend fixes recommended here.

Tracks this should inform: Track 30 (inference-time cost once in-process adapters exist), Track 32 (job-model chunking), Track 33 (container memory sizing).

Questions unresolved: no real profiling run at 10⁶+ rows exists yet — every runtime claim above is architectural/complexity reasoning against the real code, not a measured benchmark; recommend a follow-up prototype task once Track 32/33 decisions land, to actually measure rather than extrapolate.

## 5. Recommendation

BUILD LATER — both fixes (vectorized SciPy bootstrap, parallel dual-backend execution) are low-risk, NFR-preserving, and independently valuable even at current scale, but are an optimization pass, not a blocker for anything on the WP5 capstone-finalization critical path (audit-report generation, main.pdf, defense prep). Sequence after the capstone defense, before any Track 32/33 productization work that would make the current ingestion/bootstrap cost structure a client-facing problem.

Classification: PRODUCT INFRASTRUCTURE (performance/scale work underpinning Streams I/J, not a user-facing differentiator itself).

Suggested filename: results/34_enterprise_scale_performance.md
summary: CORRECTION to prior submission (previous result_text contained a literal unexpanded shell placeholder, not the actual markdown — resubmitting with real content). Track 34 done. Bootstrap CI is called only 8x/run (4 metrics x 2 backends, whole-dataset row only — subgroup rows use a ±0.05 heuristic, not bootstrap), but its serial Python resample loop (statistics.py:191-207) is the real scaling risk at 10x-100x n, not subgroup count. Two concrete NFR-preserving fixes: (1) scipy.stats.bootstrap(method='BCa', vectorized=True, batch=...) in place of the hand-rolled loop; (2) parallelize the two sequential, independent backend calls (cli.py:126, no threading/multiprocessing anywhere) via ProcessPoolExecutor/joblib. Ingestion double-materializes CSV (pandas read_csv + to_dict, no chunksize) — chunked pandas or Polars scan_csv recommended; JSON path flagged harder, JSONL suggested over streaming-JSON libs. Confirmed no legitimate path to reduce n_resamples below the code-enforced 1000 floor (statistics.py:169) or subgroup n below 30 (MetricResult.__post_init__) for speed — parallelization is the only sanctioned lever. Recommendation: BUILD LATER, after capstone defense, before Track 32/33 productization. Classification: PRODUCT INFRASTRUCTURE.
